messages.content: You are a English dementia-care education specialist. Your task is to read a caregiver-education video transcript and generate question-answer pairs that are faithful to the video, easy to understand, practically useful, and emotionally supportive for dementia caregivers. IMPORTANT: Reply strictly in English. Do not use English unless an English word appears verbatim in the input.

Read the following transcript carefully and generate the 5 most valuable question-answer pairs in English. Every QA pair must satisfy ALL FIVE quality criteria:

        Alignment (accurate & grounded): Base every answer strictly on information stated in the transcript. Do not add outside knowledge, speculate, or exaggerate. If the transcript is unclear on a point, do not create a question about it.

        Easy to Understand (clear & fluent): Write questions and answers in plain, conversational language that an 8th grade student with no medical background can understand. Define any clinical term the transcript uses. Keep answers focused — detailed enough to be complete, short enough to stay readable.

        Educational Value (actionable & useful): Prefer questions whose answers tell the caregiver what to do, why it works, or what to expect — concrete strategies, steps, and observable signs — over abstract facts. Avoid trivial or overly narrow questions.

        Supportive (empathetic): Use a warm, non-judgmental tone that normalizes the caregiver's struggles. Where the transcript offers reassurance, coping strategies, or empathy-building insight into the person with dementia's experience, capture it. Never phrase answers in a blaming or alarming way.

        Self-contained (Standalone): every pair should be read on its own, without any order, by a caregiver who has not seen the video before and can’t see the other pairs.
        Don’t mention the video, transcript or speaker.
        Name the subject in the question itself. Do not open with "this", "these", "the" + a noun the pair never names, or references that point at another pair.
        Never mention any pronouns before naming them in the same pair first.

        Coverage rules:
        - Draw questions from across the ENTIRE transcript, not just one section.
        - Ensure the pairs do not overlap significantly in content.
        - QA needs to satisfy all of the 5 criteria.

        Strictly format your response as a list of question-answer pairs, with each pair clearly marked ("Question 1: <question text>", "Timestamp 1: <range>", "Answer 1: <answer text>" on separate lines, in that order). Each transcript line begins with a [minutes:seconds] marker; on the "Timestamp N:" line, give the start-end range of the transcript section that pair is drawn from, e.g. "Timestamp 3: 4:15-6:40". Do not mention timestamps inside the question or answer text itself. Output only the structured pairs — no preamble, no closing remarks.

Question 1: How can I use a grocery list to help me remember what to buy?
Timestamp 1: 2:14-2:34
Answer 1: You can keep a written list on the counter next to the refrigerator. Whenever you run out of something or think of a new item you want, simply add it to the list. When it is time to go to the store, you will know exactly what you need to purchase.

Question 2: What is a good way to keep track of appointments and tasks for the whole week?
Timestamp 1: 2:34-2:53
Answer 2: A whiteboard is a very handy tool for this. You can use one in your office to write down the appointments and tasks you need to handle during a specific week. This allows you to see everything you need to do at a glance.

Question 3: How can I create a visual reminder that I see every day when moving between floors?
Timestamp 1: 2:53-3:16
Answer 3: You can hang a whiteboard calendar in a high-traffic area, such as a stairwell. Because it has an adhesive backing, it will not damage your walls. Since it functions like a whiteboard, you will need to wipe it clean every month and write out the activities for the next month.

Question 4: Why is it helpful to review my monthly calendar once a month?
Timestamp 1: 3:16-3:39
Answer 4: Creating a ritual to sit down once a month and look at the entire calendar helps you get the "big picture." This allows you to see all your commitments at once and helps you decide where to carve out some special time for yourself.

Question 5: What is a simple way to remind myself to do home maintenance?
Timestamp 1: 5:18-5:42
Answer 5: You can place a green bin in the middle of the kitchen to serve as a visual cue. When you see the bin, you know it is time to do maintenance. You can put all the tools and items needed for the job inside the bin. Once the project is finished, you simply put the bin away.

Question 6: What should I do if someone I am caring for has difficulty reading words?
Timestamp 1: 5:47-6:13
Answer 6: Instead of using words, you can use pictures to let them know where things are. There are many resources online where you can order kits containing stickers and signs designed to be hung around the house to provide clear visual guidance.

Question 7: Are there any digital tools that can help with reminders and appointments?
Timestamp 1: 6:27-6:52
Answer 7: Yes, there are amazing technology resources available, such as Alexa and Siri. People can talk to these systems to get information or receive verbal prompts about upcoming appointments. You can research these options online to find ones that work well for your situation.

Question 8: How can I make using memory aids more enjoyable for everyone in the house?
Timestamp 1: 6:55-7:09
Answer 8: You can have fun with the notes and keep a sense of humor in your home. Using these notes is also a wonderful way to show other people how much you care about them while helping everyone remember important things.
